      "raw_text": "The Huge 3CX Breach Was Actually 2 Linked Supply Chain Attacks | WIRED Skip to main content SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews More The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams Merch Search Andy Greenberg Security Apr 20, 2023 8:00 AM The Huge 3CX Breach Was Actually 2 Linked Supply Chain Attacks The mass compromise of the VoIP firm’s customers is the first confirmed incident where one software-supply-chain attack enabled another, researchers say. Photograph: tiero/Getty Images Save this story Save this story The cybersecurity industry has scrambled in recent weeks to understand the origins and fallout of the breach of 3CX , a VoIP provider whose software was corrupted by North Korea–linked hackers in a supply chain attack that seeded out malware to potentially hundreds of thousands of its customers. Cybersecurity firm Mandiant now has an answer to the mystery of how 3CX was penetrated by those state-sponsored hackers: The company was one of an untold number of victims infected with the corrupted software of another company—a rare, or perhaps even unprecedented, example of how a single group of hackers used one software supply chain attack to carry out a second one. Call it a supply-chain chain reaction. Today, Mandiant revealed that it found patient zero for that widespread hacking operation, which hit a significant fraction of 3CX's 600,000 customers. According to Mandiant, a 3CX employee’s PC was hacked through an earlier software-supply-chain attack that hijacked an application of the financial software firm Trading Technologies, conducted by the same hackers who compromised 3CX. That hacker group, known as Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, or Velvet Chollima, is widely believed to be working on behalf of the North Korean regime. Mandiant says the hackers somehow managed to slip backdoor code into an application available on Trading Technology's website known as X_Trader. That infected app, when it was later installed on the computer of a 3CX employee, then allowed the hackers to spread their access through 3CX's network, reach a server 3CX used for software development, corrupt a 3CX installer application, and infect a broad swath of its customers, according to Mandiant. “This is the first time we've ever found concrete evidence of a software-supply-chain attack leading to another software-supply-chain attack,” says Mandiant Consulting's chief technology officer Charles Carmakal. “So this is very big, and very significant to us.” Mandiant says it hasn't been hired by Trading Technologies to investigate the original attack that exploited its X_Trader software, so it doesn't know how the hackers altered Trading Technologies' application or how many victims—other than 3CX—there may have been from the compromise of that trading app. The company notes that Trading Technologies had stopped supporting X_Trader in 2020, though the application was still available for download through 2022. Mandiant believes, based on a digital signature on the corrupted X_Trader malware, that Trading Technologies' supply chain compromise occurred before November 2021, but that the 3CX follow-on supply chain attack didn't occur until early this year. A spokesperson for Trading Technologies told WIRED that the company had warned users for 18 months that X_Trader would no longer be supported in 2020, and that, given that X_Trader is a tool for trading professionals, there's no reason it should have been installed on a 3CX machine. The spokesperson added that 3CX was not a customer of Trading Technologies, and that any compromise of the X_Trader application doesn't affect its current software. 3CX didn't respond to WIRED's request for comment. Exactly what the North Korean hackers sought to accomplish with their interlinked software-supply-chain attacks still isn't entirely clear, but it appears to have been motivated in part by simple theft. Two weeks ago, cybersecurity firm Kaspersky revealed that at least a handful of the victims targeted with the corrupted 3CX application were cryptocurrency-related companies based in \"Western Asia,\" though it declined to name them. Kaspersky found that, as is often the case with massive software supply chain attacks, the hackers had sifted through their potential victims and delivered a piece of second-stage malware to only a tiny fraction of those hundreds of thousands of compromised networks, targeting them with “surgical precision.” Mandiant agrees that at least one goal of the North Korea–linked hackers is no doubt cryptocurrency theft: It points to earlier findings from Google's Threat Analysis Group that AppleJeus, a piece of malware tied to the same hackers, was used to target cryptocurrency services via a vulnerability in Google's Chrome browser. Mandiant also found that the same backdoor in 3CX's software was inserted into another cryptocurrency application, CoinGoTrade, and that it shared infrastructure with yet another backdoored trading app, JMT Trading. All of that, in combination with the group's targeting of Trading Technologies, points to a focus on stealing cryptocurrency, says Ben Read, Mandiant's head of cyberespionage threat intelligence. A broad supply chain attack like the one that exploited 3CX's software would “get you in places where people are handling money,” Read says. “This is a group heavily focused on monetization.” But Mandiant's Carmakal notes that given the scale of these supply chain attacks, crypto-focused victims may still be just the tip of the iceberg. “I think we'll learn about many more victims over time as it relates to one of these two software-supply-chain attacks,” he says. While Mandiant describes the Trading Technologies and 3CX compromises as the first known instance of one supply chain attack leading to another, researchers have speculated for years about whether other such incidents were similarly interlinked. The Chinese group known as Winnti or Brass Typhoon, for instance, carried out no fewer than six software-supply-chain attacks from 2016 to 2019 . And in some of those cases, the method of the hackers' initial breach wasn't ever discovered—and may well have been from an earlier supply chain attack. attack conducted via 3CXDesktopApp, a popular VoIP program. Since then, the security community has started analyzing the attack and sharing their findings. The following has been discovered so far: The infection is spread via 3CXDesktopApp MSI installers. An installer for macOS has also been trojanized. The malicious installation package contains an infected dll library that decrypts a shellcode from the d3dcompiler_47.dll library’s overlay and executes it. The decrypted payload extracts C2 server URLs from icons stored in a GitHub repository (the repository is removed). The payload connects to one of the C2 servers, downloads an infostealer and starts it. The infostealer collects system information and browser history, then sends it to the C2 server. As we reviewed available reports on the 3CX attack, we began wondering if the compromise concluded with the infostealer or further implants followed. To answer that question, we decided to review the telemetry we had on the campaign. On one of the machines, we observed a DLL named guard64.dll, which was loaded into the infected 3CXDesktopApp.exe process. Interestingly enough, we opened an investigation into a case linked to that DLL on March 21, about a week before the supply chain attack was discovered. A DLL with that name was used in recent deployments of a backdoor that we dubbed “Gopuram” and had been tracking internally since 2020. Three years ago, we were investigating an infection of a cryptocurrency company located in Southeast Asia. During the investigation, we found that Gopuram coexisted on victim machines with AppleJeus , a backdoor attributed to the Korean-speaking threat actor Lazarus . Over the years, we observed few victims compromised with Gopuram, but the number of infections began to increase in March 2023. As it turned out, the increase was directly related to the 3CX supply chain attack. We found out that the threat actor specifically targeted cryptocurrency companies, dropping the following files on infected machines: C:\\Windows\\system32\\wlbsctrl.dll, a malicious library (MD5: 9f85a07d4b4abff82ca18d990f062a84); C:\\Windows\\System32\\config\\TxR\\<machine hardware profile GUID>.TxR.0.regtrans-ms, an encrypted shellcode payload. Once dropped, wlbsctrl.dll becomes loaded on every startup by the IKEEXT service via DLL hijacking . We further saw DLLs with the names ualapi.dll and ncobjapi.dll being sideloaded into spoolsv.exe and svchost.exe, respectively. The wlbsctrl.dll library is responsible for decrypting and executing the shellcode stored in the C:\\Windows\\System32\\config\\TxR directory. The decryption is notably performed through the CryptUnprotectData API function that uses a different encryption key internally on every machine. This makes it difficult for researchers to decrypt the payload from the file without physical access to the victim machines. Snippet of the loading function using CryptUnprotectData The component loaded by the library is Gopuram’s main module. As mentioned above, its name in the export directory is guard64.dll. The job of the main module is to connect to a C2 server and request commands. The backdoor implements commands that allow the attackers to interact with the victim’s file system and create processes on the infected machine. Gopuram was additionally observed to launch in-memory modules. Just like the implants used in the 3CX campaign, Gopuram’s modules are DLL files that include an export function named DllGetClassObject. We have observed nine modules so far: Module name Description Ping Pings a host specified in the argument. Connect Connects to a given host via a socket and waits for the server to send data. Update Encrypts a provided payload and writes it to the C:\\Windows\\System32\\config\\TxR\\<machine hardware profile GUID>.TxR.0.regtrans-ms file. Net Partially implements features of the net command: management of users, groups, sessions and network shares. In our telemetry, we observed AvBugReport.exe, the executable hosting dll, to contain Gopuram’s main module payload, guard64.dll.       "raw_text": "Massive 3CX Supply-Chain Hack Targeted Cryptocurrency Firms | WIRED Skip to main content SECURITY POLITICS THE BIG STORY BUSINESS SCIENCE CULTURE REVIEWS Newsletters Security Politics The Big Story Business Science Culture Reviews More The Big Interview Magazine Events WIRED Insider WIRED Consulting Newsletters Podcasts Video Livestreams Merch Search Andy Greenberg Security Apr 3, 2023 2:03 PM The Massive 3CX Supply-Chain Hack Targeted Cryptocurrency Firms North Korean hackers appear to have used the corrupted VoIP software to go after just a handful of crypto firms with “surgical precision.” Photograph: MirageC/Getty Images Save this story Save this story Software supply-chain attacks, in which hackers corrupt widely used applications to push their own code to thousands or even millions of machines, have become a scourge, both insidious and potentially huge in the breadth of their impact. But the latest major software supply-chain attack , in which hackers who appear to be working on behalf of the North Korean government hid their code in the installer for a common VoIP application known as 3CX, seems so far to have had a prosaic goal: breaking into a handful of cryptocurrency companies. Researchers at Russian cybersecurity firm Kaspersky today revealed that they identified a small number of cryptocurrency-focused firms as at least some of the victims of the 3CX software supply-chain attack that's unfolded over the past week. Kaspersky declined to name any of those victim companies, but it notes that they're based in “western Asia.” Security firms CrowdStrike and SentinelOne last week pinned the operation on North Korean hackers, who compromised 3CX installer software that's used by 600,000 organizations worldwide, according to the vendor. Despite the potentially massive breadth of that attack, which SentinelOne dubbed “Smooth Operator,” Kaspersky has now found that the hackers combed through the victims infected with its corrupted software to ultimately target fewer than 10 machines—at least as far as Kaspersky could observe so far—and that they seemed to be focusing on cryptocurrency firms with “surgical precision.” “This was all just to compromise a small group of companies, maybe not just in cryptocurrency, but what we see is that one of the interests of the attackers is cryptocurrency companies,” says Georgy Kucherin, a researcher on Kaspersky's GReAT team of security analysts. “Cryptocurrency companies should be especially concerned about this attack because they are the likely targets, and they should scan their systems for further compromise.” Kaspersky based that conclusion on the discovery that, in some cases, the 3CX supply-chain hackers used their attack to ultimately plant a versatile backdoor program known as Gopuram on victim machines, which the researchers describe as “the final payload in the attack chain.” Kaspersky says the appearance of that malware also represents a North Korean fingerprint: It has seen Gopuram used before on the same network as another piece of malware, known as AppleJeus, linked to North Korean hackers. It's also previously seen Gopuram connect to the same command-and-control infrastructure as AppleJeus, and has seen Gopuram used previously to target cryptocurrency firms. All of that suggests not only that the 3CX attack was carried out by North Korean hackers, but that it may have been intended to breach cryptocurrency firms in order to steal from those companies, a common tactic of North Korean hackers ordered to raise money for the regime of Kim Jong-Un. It has become a recurring theme for sophisticated state-sponsored hackers to exploit software supply chains to access the networks of thousands of organizations, only to winnow their focus down to a few victims. In 2020's notorious Solar Winds spy campaign , for instance, Russian hackers compromised the IT monitoring software Orion to push malicious updates to about 18,000 victims, but they appear to have stolen data from only a few dozen of them. In the earlier supply chain compromise of the CCleaner software, the Chinese hacker group known as Barium or WickedPanda compromised as many as 700,000 PCs, but similarly chose to target a relatively short list of tech firms . “This is becoming very common,” says Kucherin, who also worked on the SolarWinds analysis and found clues linking that supply-chain attack to a known Russian group . “During supply-chain attacks, the threat actor conducts reconnaissance on the victims, collecting information, then they filter out this information, selecting victims to deploy a second-stage malware.” That filtering process is designed to help the hackers avoid detection, Kucherin points out, since deploying the second-stage malware to too many victims allows the attack to be more easily detected. But Kucherin notes that the 3CX supply-chain attack was nonetheless detected relatively quickly, compared to others. The installation of the initial malware that the hackers appeared to use for reconnaissance was detected by companies like CrowdStrike and SentinelOne last week, less than a month after it was deployed. “They tried to be stealthy, but they failed,” Kucherin says. “Their first-stage implants were discovered.” Given that detection, it's not clear how successful the campaign has been. Kucherin says Kaspersky hasn't seen any evidence of actual theft of cryptocurrency from the companies it saw targeted with the Gopuram malware. But if North Korean hackers really did compromise a piece of software used by 600,000 organizations around the world and use it just to try to steal cryptocurrency from a handful of them, they may have thrown away the keys to a much larger kingdom. “This is all unfolding very quickly. # Final Report: 2023 3CX DesktopApp Supply-Chain Compromise

## Executive summary

The public evidence supports a **two-stage, cascading software supply-chain compromise**:

1. **Initial access to 3CX** came through a prior compromise of Trading Technologies’ **X_TRADER** application. A 3CX employee installed the tampered application, which gave the attackers access to the employee’s system and enabled movement into the 3CX network. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

2. The attackers harvested credentials, moved laterally through 3CX, and compromised both its **Windows and macOS build environments**. They then corrupted a 3CX installer, causing trojanized 3CX DesktopApp releases to be distributed to customers. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

3. Mandiant tracked the activity as **UNC4736**, a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean **AppleJeus** activity. [SRC-003]

4. Kaspersky independently attributed the campaign to **Lazarus with medium-to-high confidence**, based on Gopuram’s relationship to AppleJeus, shared infrastructure and loader characteristics, and cryptocurrency targeting. This is an assessment rather than a proven identification of the operators. [SRC-004]

Public reporting also used the names **Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, and Velvet Chollima** for the activity, but the sources do not establish that all such naming conventions are universally interchangeable beyond the reporting summarized here. [SRC-008]

---

## 1. How the compromise was initiated

### Prior supply-chain compromise

Mandiant identified the initial compromise vector as malicious software downloaded from the **Trading Technologies** website. The relevant software was a tampered installer for **X_TRADER**, a Trading Technologies application. [SRC-003]

The X_TRADER compromise preceded the 3CX intrusion. WIRED reported that, based on the digital signature of the corrupted software, Mandiant believed the Trading Technologies compromise occurred before November 2021, while the follow-on 3CX compromise occurred in early 2023. [SRC-008]

The available evidence does **not** establish how the attackers originally altered the Trading Technologies software, because Mandiant had not been engaged to investigate that first compromise. [SRC-008]

### Infection of a 3CX employee system

A 3CX employee installed the infected X_TRADER application. The compromised application then enabled the attackers to access the employee’s system and spread into the broader 3CX network. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

This makes the 3CX incident a **cascading supply-chain attack**: a prior software supply-chain compromise was used to initiate a second compromise against 3CX. Mandiant described this as the first known example it had identified in which one software supply-chain attack led to another. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

---

## 2. How the intrusion propagated into 3CX’s build environment

Mandiant reconstructed the following propagation chain:

- The attackers obtained an initial foothold through the compromised X_TRADER application installed by a 3CX employee. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]
- They harvested credentials and moved laterally within the 3CX environment. [SRC-003]
- They used a compiled version of the publicly available **Fast Reverse Proxy** project for lateral movement. [SRC-003]
- They eventually compromised both the **Windows build environment** and the **macOS build environment**. [SRC-003]
- They reached the software-development/build infrastructure and corrupted a 3CX installer. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

### Windows build environment

On the Windows build environment, Mandiant identified:

- **TAXHAUL**, a launcher; and
- **COLDCAT**, a downloader.

The malware persisted through DLL search-order hijacking involving the **IKEEXT** service and ran with LocalSystem privileges. [SRC-003]

### macOS build environment

On the macOS build server, Mandiant identified **POOLRAT**, which used Launch Daemons for persistence. Mandiant stated that earlier reporting had identified the malware as SIMPLESEA, but its analysis determined that the sample was POOLRAT instead. [SRC-003]

---

## 3. How the malicious 3CX DesktopApp was distributed

The compromised build process produced a trojanized 3CX installer. The affected 3CX DesktopApp versions included **18.12.416 and earlier**. [SRC-003]

The infection chain described by the sources was:

1. A trojanized 3CX MSI or installer was distributed to customers. [SRC-004]
2. A malicious DLL decrypted shellcode from the overlay of `d3dcompiler_47.dll`. [SRC-004]
3. The malicious component obtained command-and-control server information from encrypted icon files hosted in a GitHub repository. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
4. The downloader retrieved a second-stage infostealer, identified by Mandiant as **ICONICSTEALER**. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
5. ICONICSTEALER collected browser information, including browser history and related data. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

Kaspersky also observed a more capable backdoor, **Gopuram**, in some infected systems. It identified `guard64.dll` inside the infected `3CXDesktopApp.exe` process and assessed Gopuram to be the likely principal or final payload in at least some targeted intrusions. [SRC-004]

The broad distribution of the trojanized application did not mean that every infected customer received the same follow-on payload. Kaspersky reported that Gopuram was deployed selectively, with fewer than ten such infected machines in its telemetry, and that cryptocurrency companies appeared to receive particular attention. # Final Report: 2023 3CX DesktopApp Supply-Chain Compromise

## Executive summary

The public evidence supports a **two-stage, cascading software supply-chain compromise**:

1. **Initial access to 3CX** came through a prior compromise of Trading Technologies’ **X_TRADER** application. A 3CX employee installed the tampered application, which gave the attackers access to the employee’s system and enabled movement into the 3CX network. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

2. The attackers harvested credentials, moved laterally through 3CX, and compromised both its **Windows and macOS build environments**. They then corrupted a 3CX installer, causing trojanized 3CX DesktopApp releases to be distributed to customers. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

3. Mandiant tracked the activity as **UNC4736**, a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean **AppleJeus** activity. [SRC-003]

4. Kaspersky independently attributed the campaign to **Lazarus with medium-to-high confidence**, based on Gopuram’s relationship to AppleJeus, shared infrastructure and loader characteristics, and cryptocurrency targeting. This is an assessment rather than a proven identification of the operators. [SRC-004]

Public reporting also used the names **Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, and Velvet Chollima** for the activity, but the sources do not establish that all such naming conventions are universally interchangeable beyond the reporting summarized here. [SRC-008]

---

## 1. How the compromise was initiated

### Prior supply-chain compromise

Mandiant identified the initial compromise vector as malicious software downloaded from the **Trading Technologies** website. The relevant software was a tampered installer for **X_TRADER**, a Trading Technologies application. [SRC-003]

The X_TRADER compromise preceded the 3CX intrusion. WIRED reported that, based on the digital signature of the corrupted software, Mandiant believed the Trading Technologies compromise occurred before November 2021, while the follow-on 3CX compromise occurred in early 2023. [SRC-008]

The available evidence does **not** establish how the attackers originally altered the Trading Technologies software, because Mandiant had not been engaged to investigate that first compromise. [SRC-008]

### Infection of a 3CX employee system

A 3CX employee installed the infected X_TRADER application. The compromised application then enabled the attackers to access the employee’s system and spread into the broader 3CX network. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

This makes the 3CX incident a **cascading supply-chain attack**: a prior software supply-chain compromise was used to initiate a second compromise against 3CX. Mandiant described this as the first known example it had identified in which one software supply-chain attack led to another. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

---

## 2. How the intrusion propagated into 3CX’s build environment

Mandiant reconstructed the following propagation chain:

- The attackers obtained an initial foothold through the compromised X_TRADER application installed by a 3CX employee. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]
- They harvested credentials and moved laterally within the 3CX environment. [SRC-003]
- They used a compiled version of the publicly available **Fast Reverse Proxy** project for lateral movement. [SRC-003]
- They eventually compromised both the **Windows build environment** and the **macOS build environment**. [SRC-003]
- They reached the software-development/build infrastructure and corrupted a 3CX installer. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

### Windows build environment

On the Windows build environment, Mandiant identified:

- **TAXHAUL**, a launcher; and
- **COLDCAT**, a downloader.

The malware persisted through DLL search-order hijacking involving the **IKEEXT** service and ran with LocalSystem privileges. [SRC-003]

### macOS build environment

On the macOS build server, Mandiant identified **POOLRAT**, which used Launch Daemons for persistence. Mandiant stated that earlier reporting had identified the malware as SIMPLESEA, but its analysis determined that the sample was POOLRAT instead. [SRC-003]

---

## 3. How the malicious 3CX DesktopApp was distributed

The compromised build process produced a trojanized 3CX installer. The affected 3CX DesktopApp versions included **18.12.416 and earlier**. [SRC-003]

The infection chain described by the sources was:

1. A trojanized 3CX MSI or installer was distributed to customers. [SRC-004]
2. A malicious DLL decrypted shellcode from the overlay of `d3dcompiler_47.dll`. [SRC-004]
3. The malicious component obtained command-and-control server information from encrypted icon files hosted in a GitHub repository. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
4. The downloader retrieved a second-stage infostealer, identified by Mandiant as **ICONICSTEALER**. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]
5. ICONICSTEALER collected browser information, including browser history and related data. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

Kaspersky also observed a more capable backdoor, **Gopuram**, in some infected systems. It identified `guard64.dll` inside the infected `3CXDesktopApp.exe` process and assessed Gopuram to be the likely principal or final payload in at least some targeted intrusions. [SRC-004]

The broad distribution of the trojanized application did not mean that every infected customer received the same follow-on payload. Kaspersky reported that Gopuram was deployed selectively, with fewer than ten such infected machines in its telemetry, and that cryptocurrency companies appeared to receive particular attention. [SRC-004]

---

## 4. Public attribution of the activity cluster

### Mandiant’s attribution

Mandiant tracked the campaign as **UNC4736**, described as a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean **AppleJeus** activity. [SRC-003]

Mandiant’s reasoning included:

- Similarities between the 3CX compromise and the prior Trading Technologies compromise. [SRC-003]
- Infrastructure and malware relationships involving **POOLRAT**, **CoinGoTrade**, and AppleJeus-associated activity. [SRC-003]
- A sustained focus by related activity clusters on cryptocurrency and fintech targets. [SRC-003]

Mandiant characterized the link to financially motivated North Korean operators as an assessment, not a definitive identification of a specific individual or organization. [SRC-003]

### Kaspersky’s attribution

Kaspersky attributed the campaign to **Lazarus with medium-to-high confidence**, primarily through analysis of Gopuram. Its supporting observations included:

- Gopuram had previously coexisted with AppleJeus on a Southeast Asian cryptocurrency-company system. [SRC-004]
- AppleJeus is attributed in the reporting to Lazarus. [SRC-004]
- Gopuram was used against cryptocurrency companies, consistent with Lazarus-related financially motivated activity. [SRC-004]
- A loader-shellcode pattern and the `wirexpro.com` command-and-control infrastructure overlapped with AppleJeus-related activity. [SRC-004]
- Another domain, `oilycargo.com`, had previously been attributed to Lazarus. [SRC-004]

Kaspersky therefore concluded that Lazarus was **likely** the actor deploying Gopuram, while explicitly presenting its attribution as an analytical confidence judgment. [SRC-004]

### Other public names

WIRED reported that the actor was publicly described using the names **Kimsuky, Emerald Sleet, and Velvet Chollima**, and as widely believed to operate on behalf of North Korea. [SRC-008]

The most precise cluster designation in the Mandiant evidence is **UNC4736**. The Lazarus designation is an independent Kaspersky assessment based on malware, infrastructure, targeting, and historical associations. [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

---

## 5. Evidence-chain reconstruction

```text
Trading Technologies website
        ↓
Tampered X_TRADER installer
        ↓
X_TRADER installed by a 3CX employee
        ↓
Initial access to employee system and 3CX network
        ↓
Credential harvesting and lateral movement
        ↓
Compromise of Windows and macOS 3CX build environments
        ↓
Corruption of 3CX installer
        ↓
Trojanized 3CX DesktopApp distributed to customers
        ↓
SUDDENICON / second-stage downloads
        ↓
ICONICSTEALER on broad or potential victims
        ↓
Selective deployment of Gopuram, including cryptocurrency-focused targets
```

This chain is directly supported by Mandiant’s investigation and WIRED’s summary of it. [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

---

## 6. Findings

### Finding 1

**Question:** What initiated the compromise of 3CX?

**Answer:** The initial compromise was initiated through a prior software supply-chain compromise involving a tampered Trading Technologies X_TRADER installer. A 3CX employee installed the infected application, enabling access to the 3CX network.

**Supporting entities:** Trading Technologies; X_TRADER; 3CX; 3CX employee system; Trading Technologies software supply-chain attack.

**Source references:** [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

### Finding 2

**Question:** How did the attackers reach 3CX’s build environment?

**Answer:** After gaining access through the infected X_TRADER application, the attackers harvested credentials, moved laterally using a compiled Fast Reverse Proxy project, and compromised both Windows and macOS 3CX build environments.

**Supporting entities:** UNC4736; Fast Reverse Proxy; 3CX Windows build environment; 3CX macOS build environment.

**Source references:** [SRC-003]

### Finding 3

**Question:** How was the malicious DesktopApp propagated to customers?

**Answer:** The attackers corrupted a 3CX installer in the development/build environment. The resulting trojanized 3CX DesktopApp releases were distributed through the normal software-delivery channel.

**Supporting entities:** 3CX; 3CX installer; 3CX software; SUDDENICON; ICONICSTEALER.

**Source references:** [SRC-003] [SRC-004] [SRC-008]

### Finding 4

**Question:** What was the principal technical infection chain in the distributed application?

**Answer:** The trojanized application used a malicious DLL and embedded shellcode to retrieve command-and-control information from encrypted GitHub-hosted icon files, then download ICONICSTEALER, which collected browser information.

**Supporting entities:** 3CXDesktopApp; SUDDENICON; ICONICSTEALER; GitHub.

**Source references:** [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

### Finding 5

**Question:** Was there a deeper payload beyond the infostealer?

**Answer:** Yes. Kaspersky identified Gopuram in selected infections, including cryptocurrency-related targets, and assessed it as the likely main or final payload in the attack chain observed in its telemetry.

**Supporting entities:** Gopuram; guard64.dll; 3CXDesktopApp.exe; cryptocurrency companies.

**Source references:** [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

### Finding 6

**Question:** Which threat activity cluster was publicly attributed to the campaign?

**Answer:** Mandiant tracked the campaign as UNC4736, a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed with moderate confidence that UNC4736 was related to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Kaspersky separately attributed the activity to Lazarus with medium-to-high confidence.

**Supporting entities:** UNC4736; AppleJeus; Lazarus; North Korea; Kimsuky; Emerald Sleet; Velvet Chollima.

**Source references:** [SRC-003] [SRC-004] [SRC-008]

---

## 7. Claims and confidence

- **Claim:** The 3CX compromise was initiated through a prior software supply-chain compromise involving Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER application.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

- **Claim:** A 3CX employee installed the compromised X_TRADER application, providing the path into the 3CX network.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-003] [SRC-008]

- **Claim:** The attackers moved laterally, harvested credentials, and compromised both Windows and macOS 3CX build environments.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-003]

- **Claim:** The attackers corrupted a 3CX installer and distributed trojanized DesktopApp releases to customers.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-003] [SRC-004] [SRC-008]

- **Claim:** Mandiant tracked the activity as UNC4736.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-003]

- **Claim:** Mandiant assessed that UNC4736 was related with moderate confidence to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-003]

- **Claim:** Kaspersky attributed the Gopuram-related activity to Lazarus with medium-to-high confidence.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-004]

- **Claim:** The attackers selectively deployed Gopuram, with cryptocurrency companies among the observed targets.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-004] [SRC-002]

- **Claim:** The exact original method used to compromise Trading Technologies’ X_TRADER software remains unknown in the reviewed evidence.  
  **Source references:** [SRC-008]

---

## 8. Contradictions and attribution uncertainty

### Contradiction 1: UNC4736 versus Lazarus

Mandiant’s reporting identifies the activity as **UNC4736** and describes it as a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Kaspersky separately assesses the campaign as attributable to **Lazarus** with medium-to-high confidence. These designations are compatible as a possible cluster-to-actor relationship, but the reviewed sources do not prove that UNC4736 and Lazarus are identical organizational entities.

**Source references:** [SRC-003] [SRC-004]

### Contradiction 2: SIMPLESEA versus POOLRAT

Earlier reporting identified the macOS build-server malware as SIMPLESEA. Mandiant’s subsequent analysis determined that the sample was POOLRAT instead. The later Mandiant identification should be treated as the stronger finding in the reviewed evidence, while the earlier SIMPLESEA label remains part of the reporting history.

**Source references:** [SRC-003]

### Contradiction 3: Unknown original Trading Technologies intrusion

The evidence reconstructs how the compromised X_TRADER application was used against 3CX, but it does not establish how Trading Technologies’ software was initially altered. Mandiant had not investigated that original compromise, and the number of other possible X_TRADER victims was unknown.

**Source references:** [SRC-008]

key_findings.question: What initiated the compromise of 3CX?
key_findings.answer: A prior software supply-chain compromise involving a tampered Trading Technologies X_TRADER installer. A 3CX employee installed the infected application, enabling access to the 3CX network.

key_findings.question: How did the attackers propagate into the 3CX build environment?
key_findings.answer: They harvested credentials, moved laterally using a compiled Fast Reverse Proxy project, and compromised both the Windows and macOS 3CX build environments.

key_findings.question: How was the malicious DesktopApp propagated?
key_findings.answer: The attackers corrupted a 3CX installer in the development/build environment and distributed trojanized 3CX DesktopApp releases to customers.

key_findings.question: What was the distributed application’s infection chain?
key_findings.answer: The trojanized application used malicious code and shellcode to obtain C2 information from encrypted icon files hosted on GitHub and download ICONICSTEALER, which collected browser information.

key_findings.question: Was there a deeper payload beyond the infostealer?
key_findings.answer: Kaspersky identified Gopuram in selected infections and assessed it as the likely main or final payload in the attack chain observed in its telemetry.

key_findings.question: Which threat activity cluster was publicly attributed to the campaign?
key_findings.answer: Mandiant tracked the campaign as UNC4736, a suspected North Korean nexus cluster. Mandiant assessed a moderate-confidence relationship to financially motivated North Korean AppleJeus activity. Kaspersky separately attributed the campaign to Lazarus with medium-to-high confidence.

contradictions.description: Mandiant tracked the activity as UNC4736, whereas Kaspersky assessed the campaign as attributable to Lazarus. The sources do not prove that these labels identify the same organizational entity.
Earlier reporting identified the macOS build-server malware as SIMPLESEA, but Mandiant’s later analysis determined it was POOLRAT.
The reviewed evidence identifies the compromised X_TRADER application as the initial access vector into 3CX but does not establish how Trading Technologies’ software was originally altered.

reasoning_step_details.conclusion: The 3CX incident was a cascading software supply-chain compromise rather than an isolated compromise of the 3CX build process.
The attackers’ access progressed from a 3CX employee system into 3CX development/build infrastructure.
Compromise of the build environments enabled distribution of the malicious 3CX DesktopApp.
The broad trojanized application distribution and selective Gopuram deployment represent separate stages or targeting levels within the campaign.
The strongest publicly supported cluster designation is Mandiant’s UNC4736, while Lazarus is an independent Kaspersky attribution assessment.
